steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on the new 2-D acoustic soft tactile skin (AST2), single and bi-layered. Motivate why soft tactile sensors are hard to customise, why acoustics is a good transduction route, what the earlier AST skin did, and list the contributions of this version.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Why tactile sensing matters for manipulating soft objects
2. The gap: soft sensors that are easy to prototype, cheap and customisable
3. Why current transduction methods make customisation hard
4. Separating transduction from the sensing surface; acoustics vs fluids; the AST skin
5. How AST works and what the earlier prototypes could do
6. This paper: new AST version and key contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Tactile sensing for (soft) object manipulation
- tactile sensing widely used in manipulating (soft) objects -> significant
- soft tactile sensors + tactile prediction + predictive slip control -> minimise damage; gentle interaction, essential feedback
- attributes: contact forces, shape, deformation, location, material properties -> needed by advanced control, shape execution of manipulation
- point to recent comprehensive review on tactile sensing technology

2. Gap in soft sensor design
- recent decades: big progress, many materials and transduction techniques
- gap: easy to prototype, cost-effective, customisable
- crucial when adapting to diverse shapes of end-effectors / robot components
- main challenge = transduction principle (contact properties -> measurable medium properties, e.g. voltage or current) used to infer tactile features

3. Transduction methods limit customisation
- electronic / electromagnetic: intricate circuitry under sensing surface
- changing form factor -> fabricate tailored circuitry
- camera-based: camera unit + components behind surface
- -> limits how far form factor can be minimised

4. Decoupling transduction; acoustics; AST skin
- separate transduction units from sensing surface, distinct entities
- propagating medium (acoustic waves or fluids) carries deformation info to transduction unit
- acoustics: minimal hardware for transduction unit
- demonstrated: sensorised soft pneumatic actuator, speaker + microphone inside actuator
- fluid-based systems: delayed response to tactile interactions
- acoustic sensors derive forces, contact locations, deformations, contact shapes
- but these embed electronics under the surface to emit/sense waves -> no customisation without changing electronics
- our surveys: no tactile skin without embedded circuits that allows easy customisation
- low-cost Acoustic Soft Tactile Skin (AST Skin) developed; attaches to flat and non-flat surfaces

5. How AST works; earlier version
- acoustic waves in channels beneath sensing surface carry deformation effects to transduction unit
- no electronics near soft sensing surface; acoustic components placed at convenient locations
- -> modular skins in various shapes and form factors, as long as channels can be designed underneath
- earlier work: validated only for contact normal force with 1-D contact localisation
- early prototypes: acoustic hardware attached at distal ends on a rigid casing (Fig. 1)

6. This paper and contributions
- new version of AST skin: contact normal forces, 2D contact localisation, contact geometry features (Fig. 2)
- (i) modular (2-d) skin design, acoustic hardware isolated from skin structure
- (ii) effect of multiple-layer acoustic channels on performance, sensing capabilities

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Tactile sensing is used a lot when manipulating (soft) objects, which shows that it is significant. Soft tactile sensors, especially together with tactile prediction and predictive slip control, help to minimise damage to (soft) objects during manipulation movements, because they allow gentle interactions and give essential feedback. Advanced control systems need to capture important attributes like contact forces, shape, deformation, location and material properties, and these attributes shape how manipulation tasks are executed. A more detailed exploration can be found in the recent comprehensive review on tactile sensing technology.

In the recent decades there has been a lot of progress in soft tactile sensors, and this is well documented with many different materials and transduction techniques. But there is still a gap when it comes to soft sensors that are easy to prototype, cost-effective and customisable. Such sensors are especially important when we want to adapt them to the different shapes of a robot's end-effectors or components. The main challenge in customising soft tactile sensors is their transduction principle, which is how contact properties are translated into measurable properties of a material or medium, for example electrical voltage or current measurements, and these are the basis for inferring the tactile features.

For example, soft sensors that are based on electronic or electromagnetic transduction need intricate circuitry embedded under the sensing surface. If we want to change the form factor of the sensor to fit a different shape, we need to fabricate tailored circuitry to match these changes. In the same way, sensors that use camera-based transduction have the problem that the camera unit and its components have to be accommodated behind the sensing surface. This limits how much the form factor of the sensor can be minimised.

[Decoupling transduction; acoustics; AST skin]
- separate transduction units from sensing surface, distinct entities
- propagating medium (acoustic waves or fluids) carries deformation info to transduction unit
- acoustics: minimal hardware for transduction unit
- demonstrated: sensorised soft pneumatic actuator, speaker + microphone inside actuator
- fluid-based systems: delayed response to tactile interactions
- acoustic sensors derive forces, contact locations, deformations, contact shapes
- but these embed electronics under the surface to emit/sense waves -> no customisation without changing electronics
- our surveys: no tactile skin without embedded circuits that allows easy customisation
- low-cost Acoustic Soft Tactile Skin (AST Skin) developed; attaches to flat and non-flat surfaces

[How AST works; earlier version]
- acoustic waves in channels beneath sensing surface carry deformation effects to transduction unit
- no electronics near soft sensing surface; acoustic components placed at convenient locations
- -> modular skins in various shapes and form factors, as long as channels can be designed underneath
- earlier work: validated only for contact normal force with 1-D contact localisation
- early prototypes: acoustic hardware attached at distal ends on a rigid casing (Fig. 1)

[This paper and contributions]
- new version of AST skin: contact normal forces, 2D contact localisation, contact geometry features (Fig. 2)
- (i) modular (2-d) skin design, acoustic hardware isolated from skin structure
- (ii) effect of multiple-layer acoustic channels on performance, sensing capabilities

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Tactile sensing is used a lot when manipulating (soft) objects, which shows that it is significant. Soft tactile sensors, especially together with tactile prediction and predictive slip control, help to minimise damage to (soft) objects during manipulation movements, because they allow gentle interactions and give essential feedback. Advanced control systems need to capture important attributes like contact forces, shape, deformation, location and material properties, and these attributes shape how manipulation tasks are executed. A more detailed exploration can be found in the recent comprehensive review on tactile sensing technology.

In the recent decades there has been a lot of progress in soft tactile sensors, and this is well documented with many different materials and transduction techniques. But there is still a gap when it comes to soft sensors that are easy to prototype, cost-effective and customisable. Such sensors are especially important when we want to adapt them to the different shapes of a robot's end-effectors or components. The main challenge in customising soft tactile sensors is their transduction principle, which is how contact properties are translated into measurable properties of a material or medium, for example electrical voltage or current measurements, and these are the basis for inferring the tactile features.

For example, soft sensors that are based on electronic or electromagnetic transduction need intricate circuitry embedded under the sensing surface. If we want to change the form factor of the sensor to fit a different shape, we need to fabricate tailored circuitry to match these changes. In the same way, sensors that use camera-based transduction have the problem that the camera unit and its components have to be accommodated behind the sensing surface. This limits how much the form factor of the sensor can be minimised.

One key approach to make sensor customisation easier is to separate the transduction units from the sensing surface and keep them as distinct entities. To do this, it is very effective to use a propagating medium, such as acoustic waves or fluids, to carry the information about the deformation of the sensing surface to the transduction unit. Of these options, the acoustic method has several advantages, mainly that the transduction unit needs minimal hardware components. This idea was demonstrated by sensorising a soft pneumatic actuator, where tactile features were derived using a speaker and microphone embedded inside the pneumatic actuator. There is also another reason to prefer acoustics over fluid-based methods, which is that fluid-based systems are known to have a delayed response to tactile interactions. Also, some sensors have used the acoustics method to derive tactile features like forces, contact locations, the resulting deformations and contact shapes. However these sensors have electronic components embedded below the sensing surface to emit the acoustic waves and sense the returning signals, and this limits customisation unless the electronics are changed. From our surveys we could not find any tactile skin technology like this without embedded electronic circuits that gives room for easy customisation. To address some of these shortcomings a low-cost Acoustic Soft Tactile Skin (AST Skin) has been developed. AST can be attached to flat and non-flat surfaces.

The AST skin uses acoustic waves that travel through acoustic channels placed under the sensing surface, and these transfer the effects of the sensor deformation to the transduction unit. So AST does not need electronic hardware embedded near the soft sensing surface. Instead the acoustic transduction components can be positioned at convenient locations. Because of this it is flexible, and modular skins can be made in different shapes and form factors, as long as acoustic channels can be designed under the sensing surface. In our previous work, the skin was only validated for measuring contact normal forces with 1-D contact localisation. Also, the early stage prototypes of the AST skins had the acoustic hardware attached to the distal ends on a rigid casing (see Fig. 1).

In this paper we introduce the new version of the AST skin, which is designed to measure contact normal forces with 2D contact localisation and also contact geometry features (see Fig. 2). The key contributions of this work are: (i). Developing a modular (2-d) tactile skin design that isolates the acoustic hardware components from the skin structure. (ii). Examining the impact of adding multiple-layer acoustic channels on the performance of the skin, to explore its sensing capabilities.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The widespread use of tactile sensing in manipulating (soft) objects highlights its significance. Soft tactile sensors, especially when paired with tactile prediction [1] and predictive slip control [2,3], minimise damage to (soft) objects during manipulative movements by enabling gentle interactions and providing essential feedback. Capturing crucial attributes such as contact forces, shape, deformation, location, and material properties is essential for advanced control systems, and shapes the execution of manipulation tasks [4]. For a detailed exploration, see the recent comprehensive review on tactile sensing technology [5].

In recent decades, significant strides have been made in the advancement of soft tactile sensors, as extensively documented through the use of various materials and transduction techniques [5,6]. However, a noticeable gap persists in creating soft sensors that are easy to prototype, cost-effective, and customisable. These sensors become particularly crucial when adapting to the diverse shapes of a robot's end-effectors or components. The primary challenge in customising soft tactile sensors lies in their transduction principle, which translates contact properties into measurable material or medium properties, such as electrical voltage or current measurements, that serve as the foundation for inferring tactile features.

For instance, soft sensors based on electronic or electromagnetic transduction methods require intricate circuitry embedded beneath the sensing surface [7,8,9,10,11]. Modifying the sensor's form factor to accommodate different shapes requires fabricating tailored circuitry to match these alterations. Similarly, sensors employing camera-based transduction face the challenge of accommodating the camera unit and its associated components behind the sensing surface [12,13,14]. This limitation constrains how far the sensor's form factor can be minimised.

A pivotal approach to streamlining sensor customisation is to separate the transduction units from the sensing surface, keeping them as distinct entities. To accomplish this, using a propagating medium, such as acoustic waves or fluids, to convey information about the deformation of the sensing surface to the transduction unit is highly effective. Among these options, the acoustic method presents several advantages, primarily that it requires minimal hardware components for the transduction unit. This concept was demonstrated by sensorising a soft pneumatic actuator, which derived tactile features using a speaker and microphone embedded inside the actuator [16,17,18]. There is also another reason to prefer acoustics over fluid-based methods: fluid-based systems are known for their delayed response to tactile interactions [19]. Moreover, the acoustic method has been used by certain sensors to derive tactile features such as forces [20], contact locations [21], resulting deformations [22], and contact shapes [20,23]. However, these sensors embed electronic components below the sensing surface to emit acoustic waves and sense the returning signals, which limits the possibility of customisation without altering the electronics. In our surveys, we could not find any such tactile skin technology without embedded electronic circuits that provides room for easy customisation. A low-cost Acoustic Soft Tactile Skin (AST Skin) has been developed to address some of these shortcomings. AST can be attached to flat [24] and non-flat surfaces [15].

AST skin uses acoustic waves travelling through acoustic channels positioned beneath the sensing surface to transfer the effects of sensor deformation to the transduction unit. AST does not need electronic hardware embedded near the soft sensing surface; instead, the acoustic transduction components can be positioned at convenient locations. This provides the flexibility to create modular skins in various shapes and form factors, as long as acoustic channels can be designed beneath the sensing surface. In [15], the skin was only validated for measuring contact normal forces with 1-D contact localisation. Moreover, the early stage prototypes of the AST skins had the acoustic hardware attached to the distal ends on a rigid casing (see Fig. 1).

This paper introduces a new version of the AST skin, designed to measure contact normal forces with 2D contact localisation as well as contact geometry features (see Fig. 2). The key contributions of this work are: (i). Development of a modular (2-d) tactile skin design that strategically isolates the acoustic hardware components from the skin structure. (ii). Examination of the impact of incorporating multiple-layer acoustic channels on the skin's performance, thereby exploring its sensing capabilities.
